heading: Unmasking among autistic university students
sample: 14 interviews + 214 surveys of autistic university students
text: Autistic masking or camouflaging describes the efforts some autistic people make to hide, modify or compensate for autistic traits in order to fit social expectations. It can include deliberately controlling eye contact, imitating other people's behaviour, following social scripts, filtering what one wants to say, or suppressing movements and responses linked to sensory needs.

This study examined a related but different phenomenon: **unmasking**, understood as a deliberate effort to reduce or stop masking strategies after using them for a prolonged period. The research combined interviews with 14 autistic university students and a survey of 214 students.

Most participants were familiar with the concept of unmasking and about half had tried to put it into practice. Experiences varied greatly between people. For some, it was relatively possible to stop hiding certain behaviours or needs. For others, masking had become so internalised that it was difficult to tell which behaviours were spontaneous and which had been learned in order to fit in.

Participants described benefits related to a stronger sense of authenticity and relief from the continual effort of monitoring their own behaviour. However, unmasking also brought uncertainty and fear of possible social consequences, such as rejection, misunderstanding or loss of acceptance. Context mattered: people tended to feel more able to behave authentically with trusted friends, with other autistic people, or in settings where they perceived acceptance.

In the survey, greater difficulty unmasking was associated with higher anxiety. Unmasking with family was associated with lower symptoms of anxiety and depression, although other associations were less consistent.

The study suggests that reducing masking may be linked to authenticity and stress relief for some people, but it is not a simple process and is not necessarily safe in every setting. Social acceptance and support from other people appear to matter substantially.
It does not show that every autistic person should stop masking, that doing so always reduces anxiety or depression, or that it is safe in every social, educational or work context.
notProven: It does not show that every autistic person should stop masking, that doing so always reduces anxiety or depression, or that it is safe in every context.
linea: Mixed-methods study with 14 interviews + 214 surveys of autistic university students. It does not show that every autistic person should stop masking, that doing so always reduces anxiety or depression, or that it is safe in every context.

heading: GGOC-AD and OCD-related beliefs in adolescents
design: Randomised controlled trial with active comparator
sample: 94 adolescents; 48 intervention and 46 active comparator; 14 days + one-month follow-up
text: Maladaptive beliefs related to obsessive-compulsive disorder —for example, excessive responsibility, overestimation of threat, perfectionism, intolerance of uncertainty, or the need to control thoughts— are part of cognitive models used to explain how some obsessive experiences can be maintained or intensified.

The study evaluated GGOC-AD, an unguided mobile intervention designed to address these beliefs in adolescents from the Spanish general population. Ninety-four students took part. Forty-eight used GGOC-AD and 46 used a comparison app with neutral content for 14 days. The groups were assessed before the intervention, immediately afterwards and one month later.

Compared with the control group, participants using GGOC-AD had significantly lower scores on several dimensions of obsessive-compulsive beliefs: responsibility and threat estimation, perfectionism and intolerance of uncertainty, and the importance of and need to control thoughts. They also had lower obsessive-compulsive symptom scores.

Effect sizes were small to moderate. The largest effect among the beliefs examined concerned the importance attributed to thoughts and the need to control them. The effect on OCD symptom scores was also small to moderate.
No significant differences were found between groups in anxiety, depression or self-esteem.
The results indicate that a brief mobile intervention can change certain OCD-related beliefs in the short term and reduce obsessive-compulsive symptom scores in community adolescents.

It does not show that the app prevents OCD in the long term, replaces clinical treatment, or produces general improvements in anxiety, depression or self-esteem. The sample was relatively small and follow-up was brief.
notProven: It does not demonstrate long-term prevention of OCD, it does not replace clinical treatment, and follow-up was brief.
linea: Randomised controlled trial with an active comparator involving 94 adolescents; 48 intervention and 46 active comparator; 14 days + one-month follow-up. It does not demonstrate long-term prevention of OCD, it does not replace clinical treatment, and follow-up was brief.

heading: Sleep and anxiety in adolescents
text: This meta-analysis examined how different aspects of sleep relate to anxiety during adolescence. It brought together cross-sectional studies, longitudinal research and randomised controlled trials, allowing the authors to examine not only whether sleep and anxiety are associated at the same point in time, but also whether sleep problems precede later changes in anxiety and whether changing sleep can influence anxiety.

In cross-sectional analyses, poorer overall sleep quality showed a moderate association with higher anxiety. The overall correlation was approximately **r = 0.34**. Sleep disturbance and poorer daytime functioning showed associations of similar or slightly greater magnitude. Difficulty falling asleep showed a smaller relationship. Short sleep duration and a more evening-oriented circadian preference were also related to anxiety, although the associations were weaker.

Longitudinal studies indicated that poorer sleep quality at baseline could predict higher anxiety later. This predictive relationship was clearer over follow-up periods of up to about 12 months. Short sleep duration produced less consistent findings than sleep quality.

Randomised trials added another relevant finding: manipulations that worsened sleep increased anxiety levels, while interventions intended to improve sleep —including insomnia interventions— were associated with reductions in anxiety.

Taken together, the evidence indicates that **sleep quality is one of the factors most consistently related to adolescent anxiety within this meta-analysis**. The longitudinal and experimental findings make the evidence more informative than a simple cross-sectional correlation.
Not every sleep problem causes anxiety, and not all anxiety is explained by sleep. The studies used different measures and designs, and a substantial part of the literature remains observational.
notProven: Not every sleep problem causes anxiety, and not all anxiety is explained by sleep. A substantial part of the literature remains observational.
linea: Meta-analysis with 129 independent samples and 416,426 adolescents. Not every sleep problem causes anxiety, and not all anxiety is explained by sleep. A substantial part of the literature remains observational.

heading: Receiving an ADHD diagnosis in adulthood
authors: Lucy McGill, Isabella Jardim-Lalor and Cliodhna O’Connor
text: This systematic review brought together research on how people experience receiving an ADHD diagnosis in adulthood. Its aim was not to determine treatment effectiveness or measure ADHD prevalence, but to synthesise personal experiences associated with the diagnostic process.
The authors identified three broad areas: **the relationship with oneself, the relationship with other people, and the relationship with care systems**.

In relation to the self, many people described diagnosis as an important event for reinterpreting their own biography. Past behaviours, difficulties and experiences could take on a new meaning. For some, this supported self-understanding and a more compassionate attitude towards themselves. At the same time, people could also experience grief, anger, frustration at not having been identified earlier, or confusion about their own identity.

In social relationships, diagnosis could help relatives, partners or friends understand certain needs or behaviours better. However, it also introduced concerns about stigma and about whether or not to disclose the diagnosis.

In relation to healthcare systems, many studies described delays, barriers and complex pathways to assessment. Support after diagnosis varied greatly: some people received treatment, information or follow-up, while others felt that the process effectively ended when they received the diagnostic label.

Receiving an ADHD diagnosis in adulthood can be both **validating and destabilising**. Its impact depends on personal history, relationships, social context, stigma and the resources available after diagnosis.
The review does not show what proportion of adults experiences each reaction and cannot predict how a particular person will experience their diagnosis.
notProven: It does not show what proportion of adults experiences each reaction and cannot predict how a particular person will experience their diagnosis.
linea: Systematic review with thematic synthesis covering 21 studies and 397 participants. It does not show what proportion of adults experiences each reaction and cannot predict how a particular person will experience their diagnosis.

heading: ARFID compared with anorexia and bulimia in young people
text: ARFID is an eating disorder characterised by insufficient or highly restricted intake that is not explained by a central concern about body weight or shape, as is commonly seen in anorexia nervosa. Avoidance may be related, among other reasons, to sensitivity to tastes or textures, low interest in food, or fear of negative consequences such as choking or vomiting.
This review compared the clinical profile of children and adolescents with ARFID with that of young people with anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa.

Compared with anorexia nervosa, the ARFID group had a higher likelihood of anxiety and a lower likelihood of depressive disorders. ARFID samples also included a substantially higher proportion of boys, had a lower mean age and recorded fewer hospital admissions.

A similar pattern appeared in several respects when ARFID was compared with bulimia nervosa. Depressive disorders were less frequent in ARFID and the proportion of boys was clearly higher. People with ARFID were also younger. Anxiety tended to be more frequent in ARFID than in bulimia, although that difference did not reach statistical significance in the relevant analysis.

The data support the conclusion that ARFID has a different clinical profile from anorexia and bulimia in young people. That distinction matters because it helps avoid interpreting every form of restricted eating through the same model.

It does not mean that every person with ARFID is young, male or anxious, or that hospital admission can never be necessary. The findings come from clinical studies using different criteria and samples.
notProven: It does not mean that every person with ARFID is young, male or anxious, or that hospital admission can never be necessary.
linea: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 22 studies. It does not mean that every person with ARFID is young, male or anxious, or that hospital admission can never be necessary.

heading: Stigma in adults with ADHD
authors: Thilaanee Krishnamoorthy, Soumitra Das and Naveen Thomas
text: The review examined the different forms of stigma described by adults with ADHD and their possible relationship with quality of life. The included studies addressed **self-stigma or internalised stigma, perceived stigma, public stigma and structural stigma**.

Internalised stigma was related to negative self-evaluations and to taking on disparaging social messages about ADHD. Greater ADHD symptom severity was associated with more internalised stigma, which in turn was related to greater functional impairment, lower self-esteem and poorer quality of life.
Perceived stigma —the expectation or perception of being judged by other people— was linked to difficulties seeking help, following medication treatment or deciding whether to disclose the diagnosis.

Public stigma was the most studied type. The research described negative social attitudes, stereotypes and judgements about people with ADHD, with a particular concentration of studies in academic settings.

Structural stigma was studied far less. The limited available research described barriers to accessing care, but the review found very little work directly measuring how those barriers affect quality of life.
There is a consistent evidence base documenting different forms of stigma towards adults with ADHD. Evidence is especially clear for self-stigma, perceived stigma and public stigma.
The review does not establish a causal relationship between stigma and poorer quality of life, and it notes that structural stigma remains under-researched.
notProven: It does not establish causality between stigma and quality of life, and shows that evidence on structural barriers remains limited.
linea: Systematic review of 17 studies. It does not establish causality between stigma and quality of life, and shows that evidence on structural barriers remains limited.

heading: Developmental dyslexia and DLD together
text: The study examined reading when developmental dyslexia and developmental language disorder occur together.

The co-occurring group showed broader and more severe reading difficulties affecting decoding, fluency and comprehension. Dyslexia alone tended to affect decoding more, while DLD alone tended to affect language comprehension more.
notProven: It does not determine how often the two conditions co-occur in the general population, and the studies used different criteria and measures.
linea: PRISMA systematic review of 18 studies. It does not determine how often the two conditions co-occur in the general population, and the studies used different criteria and measures.

heading: Obsessions and compulsions in adolescents with OCD
text: OCD includes obsessions and compulsions, but these two components are not exactly the same. This study investigated whether the severity of obsessions and the severity of compulsions were related to different patterns of brain connectivity in adolescents.

Forty adolescents with OCD and 40 matched controls without OCD took part. The researchers used functional MRI and whole-brain connectivity analyses. They also compared the resulting maps with information on neurotransmitter receptor distribution and gene expression.
Within the OCD group, obsessions and compulsions were related to one another, but only moderately, supporting the decision to analyse them as partly distinct dimensions.

The severity of obsessions was related to connectivity patterns involving, among other regions, the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and posterior areas of the cerebellum. Some of those patterns included connections with the default mode, visual and sensorimotor networks.
Analyses of compulsions showed different associations, leading the authors to propose that obsessions and compulsions may rely partly on different neural circuits.
The study provides exploratory evidence that separating obsessions and compulsions as dimensions may help researchers study the heterogeneity of adolescent OCD more precisely.

It does not identify a diagnostic biomarker. This study does not support using a brain scan to diagnose OCD, predict the right treatment or determine the severity of an individual person's condition. The sample was small and the work is exploratory.
notProven: It does not identify a diagnostic biomarker. This study does not support using a brain scan to diagnose OCD or choose treatment for an individual person.
linea: Exploratory neuroimaging study with 40 adolescents with OCD + 40 controls. It does not identify a diagnostic biomarker. This study does not support using a brain scan to diagnose OCD or choose treatment for an individual person.

heading: Body representations in autistic people
text: Body representation is not a single process. It includes, among other dimensions, the **body schema**, which contributes to movement and sensorimotor regulation, and **body image**, which includes conscious, perceptual, emotional and cognitive experience of one's own body.

The review examined how these dimensions were studied in autistic people between 2000 and 2025. One of the clearest findings was the strong imbalance in the literature: about 81% of the studies focused on body schema and sensorimotor aspects, while body image was studied far less.
The themes studied included interoception, proprioception, multisensory integration and other processes related to how the brain integrates signals from the body and the environment.

The review did not find a single alteration that would justify speaking of a general 'autistic body deficit'. Results varied according to the dimension assessed, the task used, age and sample characteristics.
The authors propose that studying body representations in a more organised way may help understanding of sensory perception, motor coordination, autonomy, self-perception and identity.
The available research suggests that body representations in autism are **multidimensional** and cannot be reduced to one ability.
There is no single body-related alteration present in every autistic person. The literature is very uneven and some dimensions have barely been studied.
notProven: There is no single 'autistic body deficit' and no body-related alteration present in every autistic person.
linea: Systematic review of 54 studies and 2,982 participants. There is no single 'autistic body deficit' and no body-related alteration present in every autistic person.

heading: Mental imagery, sensory sensitivity and autistic traits
text: The study examined three variables: the intensity or vividness of mental imagery, sensory sensitivity and autistic traits. The sample included autistic and non-autistic adults, and standardised questionnaires were used to assess visual and tactile mental imagery, sensory sensitivity and autistic traits.
As expected from previous research, autistic traits showed a strong association with sensory sensitivity: higher autistic-trait scores were related to higher sensory-sensitivity scores.
Higher autistic-trait scores were also associated with somewhat less vivid mental imagery in both visual and tactile modalities. However, these associations were small.

The central finding was that the relationship between mental imagery and sensory sensitivity was minimal. The association between visual imagery and sensory sensitivity was very small and would no longer be statistically significant after a strict correction for multiple comparisons. No significant association was found between tactile imagery and sensory sensitivity.
Autistic participants in the sample were also more likely than non-autistic participants to have scores compatible with aphantasia —very weak or absent visual mental imagery.

The data support a clear relationship between autistic traits and sensory sensitivity, but do not support the idea that the vividness of mental imagery is an important explanation for that sensitivity.
This was a cross-sectional study using self-report measures. It cannot establish causation or apply its findings to a particular individual.
notProven: It is cross-sectional and based on self-report; it does not establish causation or explain an individual person's sensory sensitivity.
linea: Online cross-sectional study of 595 adults. It is cross-sectional and based on self-report; it does not establish causation or explain an individual person's sensory sensitivity.
